nodes.summary: Let $0 < k \le n$. The number of hash sequences $f : \{0, \dots, k-1\} \to \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ for which linear probing without wrap-around places all $k$ items in a table of $n$ cells (without overflow) is
nodes.title: Number of hash sequences without overflow

nodes.summary: Let $1 \le n \le N$ and let $c$ be a cell of a cyclic table of $N$ cells. Exactly $(N - n)\,N^{n-1}$ of the $N^n$ hash sequences of $n$ items leave $c$ empty after linear probing, a fraction $(N - n)/N$. For $N = 3$ and $n = 2$, three of the nine sequences leave cell $0$ empty; the Lean tests check this by enumeration.
nodes.title: Number of hash sequences that leave a given cell empty

nodes.summary: If a hash sequence has at most $N$ items, linear probing in a cyclic table of $N$ cells places each item in its own cell: the set of occupied cells has exactly as many elements as there are items.
nodes.title: Linear probing places every item while the table has room

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be the set of occupied cells of a cyclic table of $N$ cells $0, \dots, N - 1$. Starting at cell $h$, this counts the consecutive occupied cells $h, h + 1, h + 2, \dots$ (indices modulo $N$) met before the first empty cell, examining at most a given number of cells (the budget). The recursion is on the budget; the displacement uses the budget $N$.
nodes.title: Linear-probing scan with a probe budget

nodes.summary: In an empty table, the displacement of an item is $0$ whatever its hash address: the first cell examined is empty.
nodes.title: An insertion into an empty table has displacement zero

nodes.summary: In a cyclic table of $N$ cells whose occupied cells form $S$, the displacement of an item with hash address $h$ is the number of occupied cells $h, h + 1, \dots$ (indices modulo $N$) that it passes over before it reaches an empty cell. It is computed by the scan with a probe budget with budget $N$, so it is at most $N$. When the table is not full it is the distance from $h$ to the first empty cell.
nodes.title: Displacement of a linear-probing insertion

nodes.summary: If fewer than $N$ of the $N$ cells are occupied, the cell taken by an insertion is empty, whatever the hash address: the scan from the hash address meets an empty cell within $N$ steps.
nodes.title: An insertion into a table that is not full lands on an empty cell

nodes.summary: An item with hash address $h$, entered into a cyclic table whose occupied cells form $S$, falls into cell $h + d \bmod N$, where $d$ is its displacement.
nodes.title: Cell taken by a linear-probing insertion

nodes.summary: Let $1 \le k \le N$. Enter $k$ items into a cyclic table of $N$ cells by linear probing, with independent uniform hash addresses. The expected number of probes made by the $k$-th item is
nodes.title: Knuth's exact mean insertion cost for linear probing

nodes.summary: For every table size $N > 0$, the expected cost of an insertion into the empty table is $1$: Knuth's $M(N, 1) = 1$.
nodes.title: Inserting into an empty table costs one probe

nodes.summary: Let $N$ and $n$ be natural numbers. Consider all $N^{n+1}$ hash sequences $a_1, \dots, a_{n+1}$ with values in the $N$ cells of a cyclic table, each equally likely. For each of them, enter the first $n$ items by linear probing and count the probes made by the last one. The expected cost is the average of this count, a rational number.
nodes.title: Expected cost of a linear-probing insertion

nodes.title: Knuth's auxiliary sums for linear probing

nodes.summary: Let $n \le N$ and let $c$ be a cell of a cyclic table of $N$ cells. Then
nodes.title: Rotational symmetry of linear probing

nodes.summary: Rotate every hash address of a sequence by $j$ cells, $a_i \mapsto a_i + j \bmod N$. Then the occupied cells after linear probing are those of the original sequence rotated by $j$ cells. Linear probing treats all cells of the cyclic table alike; this is the "circular symmetry" on which Knuth's 1963 proof of Lemma 1 and the 1998 analysis of linear probing rest.
nodes.title: Linear probing commutes with rotations of the table

nodes.summary: For a hash sequence $a_1, \dots, a_k$ with values in the cells $0, \dots, N - 1$ of a cyclic table, this is the set of occupied cells after the items are entered in order by linear probing, starting from the empty table. Each item goes to the cell given by its hash address and the cells already occupied.
nodes.title: Occupied cells after a hash sequence

nodes.summary: In an empty table, an insertion makes exactly one probe, whatever its hash address.
nodes.title: An insertion into an empty table makes one probe

nodes.summary: The number of probes of an insertion with hash address $h$ into a cyclic table whose occupied cells form $S$ is its displacement plus one. In Knuth's 1963 description of the algorithm, it is the number of times the comparison step "if $x_j = 0$, set $x_j = 1$ and stop" is executed: once for each occupied cell passed over, and once for the empty cell that receives the item.
nodes.title: Probes of a linear-probing insertion

nodes.summary: Let $1 \le k \le N$. In a cyclic table of $N$ cells holding $k$ items inserted by linear probing with independent uniform hash addresses, the average cost of a successful search is
nodes.title: Knuth's exact mean successful-search cost for linear probing

nodes.summary: For every table size $N > 0$, the expected cost of a successful search in a table holding one item is $1$: Knuth's $T(N, 1) = 1$.
nodes.title: A table holding one item is searched in one probe

nodes.summary: For a table of $N$ cells built from $n$ uniformly random hash addresses, this is $T(N, n) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} M(N, i + 1)$, the average over the stored items of the expected cost of their insertion. nodes.title: Expected cost of a successful linear-probing search

nodes.summary: Let $0 \le \alpha < 1$, and let a cyclic table of $N$ cells hold $n_N$ items, where $n_N < N$ for all large $N$ and $n_N / N \to \alpha$. Then the expected number of probes to insert one more item, which is also the expected cost of an unsuccessful search, satisfies
nodes.title: Expected cost of an unsuccessful linear-probing search at a fixed load factor

nodes.summary: Let $r$ be a natural number and $0 \le \alpha < 1$. If $n_N / N \to \alpha$ as $N \to \infty$, then Knuth's sums satisfy
nodes.title: Limit of Knuth's sums at a fixed load factor

nodes.summary: Let $0 \le \alpha < 1$, and let a cyclic table of $N$ cells hold $n_N$ items, where $1 \le n_N \le N$ for all large $N$ and $n_N / N \to \alpha$. Then the average cost of a successful search satisfies
nodes.title: Expected cost of a successful linear-probing search at a fixed load factor
Combinatorics

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
